questions.explanation: Kleppmann's distinction is about where the hard problems live: data-intensive apps wrestle with data volume, complexity, and velocity. Running on many machines or using a relational database are implementation details, and heavy floating-point work describes compute-intensive applications like scientific simulation.
options: It runs on a cluster of many machines instead of a single server
Its main challenges are the amount, complexity, and speed of change of data
It stores all of its data in a relational database
It performs more floating-point operations per second
questions.question: What makes an application "data-intensive" rather than "compute-intensive"?

questions.explanation: The book's examples are Redis (a datastore) used as a message queue and Kafka (a message queue) offering database-like durability. Storing rows in tables is the textbook use of a relational database, while CDNs and load balancers are doing exactly their traditional jobs — no category boundary is crossed.
options: Using Redis as a message queue
Using a relational database to store rows in tables
Using a CDN to cache static images at the edge
Using a load balancer to spread HTTP requests across servers
questions.question: Which example best illustrates that the boundaries between categories of data systems are blurring?

questions.explanation: A fault is one component deviating from its spec (the dead disk); a failure is the system as a whole not working. The RAID tolerated the fault, so users saw no failure. The first option reverses the terms, and the last is wrong because the disk genuinely deviated from its spec.
options: A failure occurred, but not a fault
Both a fault and a failure occurred
A fault occurred, but not a failure
Neither a fault nor a failure occurred
questions.question: A disk in a RAID array fails, but the storage service keeps serving reads and writes with no user-visible impact. In the book's terminology, what happened?

questions.explanation: Hardware faults are random and uncorrelated — that is precisely why redundancy works against them, ruling out the first option. But a software bug is systematic: every replica runs the same code, so all of them hit the same bug. The defense is careful design and testing, not more copies or bigger machines.
options: Hardware faults are correlated, so replicas tend to fail together
Redundancy was configured incorrectly
Software faults are systematic: the same bug strikes every replica, so redundancy alone cannot fix them
The replicas should have been scaled up to more powerful machines
questions.question: A team runs three replicas of its database so that one machine failure will not cause downtime. A bug in the storage engine then corrupts data identically on all three replicas. What does this demonstrate?

questions.explanation: Load parameters describe the load itself — request rate, read/write ratio, concurrent users, data volume. p99 latency is a performance metric, CPU cores describe resources, and uptime describes availability; the book insists on keeping these categories distinct when reasoning about scalability.
options: p99 response time of 120 ms
Requests per second and the ratio of reads to writes
The number of CPU cores on each server
The percentage of uptime over the last quarter
questions.question: Which of the following is a load parameter?

questions.explanation: The mean hides outliers, but users feel them: with fan-out, one slow backend call delays the whole page. The first option is backwards — percentiles cost more to compute than a mean. The last reverses the book's point: tail latency matters most for interactive, user-facing services.
options: Percentiles are cheaper to compute than averages
Averages are mathematically undefined for response times
Slow outliers disproportionately hurt users — e.g., a page that fans out to many services waits for the slowest one
Tail latency only matters for batch processing, not interactive services
questions.question: Why does the book recommend reporting response times as high percentiles (e.g., p95, p99) instead of the mean?

questions.explanation: Reliability, scalability, and maintainability are the chapter's three lenses. The first option is the CAP theorem — a real but different framework about distributed trade-offs. Throughput, latency, and cost are useful metrics and normalization/indexing/sharding are techniques, not the chapter's organizing concerns.
options: Consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
Throughput, latency, and cost
Reliability, scalability, and maintainability
Normalization, indexing, and sharding
questions.question: Chapter 1 proposes three concerns for evaluating the design of any data-intensive application. What are they?

questions.explanation: The book stresses that demanding applications need a mix of tools — databases, caches, search indexes, stream and batch processors — integrated via application code. Standardizing on one tool contradicts this directly, and Kafka refutes the last option by offering database-like durability despite being a message queue.
options: A single tool rarely meets all of an application's data needs, so applications combine several specialized tools
Different tools are typically glued together through application code
Every application should standardize on exactly one data system to avoid complexity
Message queues never offer durability guarantees
questions.question: Which statements about modern data systems are true? (Select all that apply.)

questions.explanation: The book's list: minimize error opportunities, decouple error-prone actions from the failure blast radius, test thoroughly at all levels, allow fast recovery, set up detailed monitoring, and enforce good management practices. Giving everyone production access does the opposite — it widens the blast radius of any single mistake.
options: Design systems to minimize opportunities for error
Decouple the places where people make mistakes from the places where failures can occur
Allow quick and easy recovery from human errors
Give every engineer direct production access so problems get fixed faster
questions.question: Studies cited in the chapter found that configuration errors by operators cause many outages. Which practices reduce the risk from human error? (Select all that apply.)

questions.explanation: Reliability means correct behavior in the face of adversity — including bad inputs and attackers — not the absence of adversity. The last option states the key misconception the chapter rejects: faults are inevitable, so the goal is tolerating them without user-visible failure.
options: A reliable system keeps performing its expected function correctly even when faults occur
Reliability includes preventing unauthorized access and misuse
A reliable system tolerates users making mistakes or using it in unexpected ways
A reliable system is one in which faults never happen
questions.question: Which statements about reliability are true? (Select all that apply.)

questions.explanation: The first option is the standard scale-up versus scale-out distinction, the second restates the chapter's two key scalability questions, and the third defines elastic systems. The last contradicts the chapter: means hide the tail-latency outliers that determine whether growth actually preserves the user experience.
options: Scaling up means moving to a more powerful machine; scaling out means distributing load across more machines
To reason about scalability, describe load with load parameters and ask how performance changes as load grows with fixed resources, and how many resources are needed to hold performance constant
An elastic system can automatically add computing resources when it detects a load increase
The mean response time is the best single number for judging whether a system scales
questions.question: Which statements about scalability are correct? (Select all that apply.)

questions.explanation: These map to the chapter's three aspects of maintainability: operability (easy to run and observe), simplicity (manage complexity with abstractions, avoid tight coupling and hacks), and evolvability (requirements change, so make change cheap). The last option is the opposite of simplicity — tight coupling makes every change risky.
options: Making the system easy to monitor and debug in production
Using good abstractions to hide complexity and avoid tight coupling
Designing so that changing requirements are easy to accommodate
Tightly coupling components so one change propagates everywhere automatically
questions.question: Which practices support maintainability? (Select all that apply.)

summary.overview: Chapter 1 sets up the vocabulary for the entire book: most modern applications are data-intensive rather than compute-intensive, and every data system should be judged by whether it is reliable (works correctly despite faults), scalable (handles growth gracefully), and maintainable (teams can operate, understand, and evolve it). These three concerns are the lens through which the rest of the book examines data models, storage engines, and encoding.

sections.heading: Thinking About Data Systems
takeaways: Modern applications are data-intensive rather than compute-intensive: the hard problems are the amount, complexity, and speed of change of data.
The boundaries between categories of data systems are blurring — e.g., Redis (a datastore) is used as a message queue, while Kafka (a message queue) offers database-like durability.
No single tool meets all of an application's data needs, so applications combine databases, caches, search indexes, and stream/batch processors, usually integrated through application code.

sections.heading: Reliability
takeaways: Reliability means the system keeps performing its expected function correctly even in the face of adversity; a fault is one component deviating from its spec, while a failure is the system as a whole not working.
Hardware faults tend to be random and uncorrelated, which is why redundancy (extra machines, RAID) is an effective defense against them.
Software faults are systematic and correlated — the same bug strikes every replica at once — so the defense is careful design and thorough testing, not just more copies.

Human error, often configuration mistakes, causes a large share of outages; reduce it by minimizing opportunities for error, decoupling error-prone actions from failure blast radius, testing at all levels, enabling quick recovery, monitoring, and good management practices.
Reliability also covers security: preventing unauthorized access and misuse, and tolerating users who make mistakes or use the system in unexpected ways.

sections.heading: Scalability
takeaways: Scalability is meaningless without specifics: describe load with load parameters (requests/sec, read/write ratio, concurrent users, data volume), then ask how performance changes as load grows with fixed resources, and how many resources are needed to hold performance constant as load grows.

Report response times as high percentiles (p95, p99), not the mean — tail latency matters because slow outliers disproportionately hurt users, e.g., a page fanning out to many services waits for the slowest one.

Two generic ways to cope with growth: scaling up (a more powerful machine) versus scaling out (distributing load across more machines); elastic systems add resources automatically when load increases.

sections.heading: Maintainability
takeaways: Operability: make the system easy to run — monitorable and debuggable, easy to upgrade, with capacity planning, documentation, good defaults, no dependency on individual machines, and predictable behavior.
Simplicity: manage complexity with good abstractions; avoid large state spaces, tight coupling, hacks, and inconsistencies that make the system hard to understand.
Evolvability: requirements change, so design for easy adaptation rather than assuming the system will ever be finished.

sections.heading: Summary
takeaways: Judge any data system with three questions: does it stay reliable under faults, can it scale with growth, and can teams maintain and evolve it productively?
Faults are inevitable, so aim for fault tolerance (no user-visible failure), not fault absence; describe load precisely, watch tail latency, and keep designs simple and adaptable.
